_説明: English explanations shown when you click a word in code while reading in English. Same keys as glossary.json. A first line "Origin: ..." is shown folded in the speech bubble. Words missing here fall back to the Japanese glossary.json.
train_test_split:
A function that splits data into a "training" part and a "test" part. Used to check accuracy on data not used for training.
It returns four things: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test.
train_test_split.test_size:
The share of data set aside for testing. 0.3 means 30% for testing and the remaining 70% for training.
An integer (for example 50) means "50 items".
train_test_split.random_state:
The seed of the random numbers that decide the split. With the same number (for example 0), you get the same split every run, so results are easy to compare.
If omitted, the split differs every time.
train_test_split.stratify:
Stratification. Keeps the share of each label the same in the training and test sets.
With stratify=y, the shares in y (for example still 50%, walking 30%, running 20%) are almost the same in both.
Prevents accidents where some label is missing from the test set when there is little data or the labels are uneven.
train_test_split.shuffle: Whether to shuffle the data before splitting. The default is True. Use False when you want the first part of a time series for training and the later part for testing.
DecisionTreeClassifier:
A model that classifies with a decision tree. It decides with combinations of if statements such as "if the mean of x is 0.5 or less...".
Since it is made of if statements, it is easy to move to the Pico.
DecisionTreeClassifier.max_depth:
The maximum depth of the tree (how deeply the if statements nest).
Smaller makes the model small and simple, and easy to fit on the Pico. Too large and it memorizes the training data (overfitting) and misses on new data.
DecisionTreeClassifier.random_state: The seed of the random numbers used during training. With the same number, you get the same tree every time.
DecisionTreeClassifier.min_samples_leaf: The minimum number of data items needed in one leaf (result). Larger values make overly fine branches less likely.
random_state: A random seed. With the same number, you get the same result every run.
fit: Trains the model. fit(X, y) means "learn to predict y (the correct labels) from X (the features)".
predict: Classifies with the trained model. predict(X) returns the label for each row of X.
classification_report:
A function that turns classification scores into text for display. classification_report(correct, predicted).
For each label it shows precision (share correct), recall (share not missed), f1-score (the balance of the two) and support (number of items).
Pin:
A class for using a pin (GPIO). Written as Pin(number, direction, pull-up).
For example Pin(25, Pin.OUT) makes pin 25 an output, and Pin(24, Pin.IN, Pin.PULL_UP) makes pin 24 an input.
Pin.OUT: Makes the pin an output. It can output 0 V or 3.3 V (to light an LED and so on).
Pin.IN: Makes the pin an input. It can read 0 or 1 (a button and so on).
Pin.PULL_UP:
Pull-up. A resistor inside the Pico makes the value 1 when nothing is connected.
If you connect a button between the pin and GND, it reads 1 when not pressed and 0 when pressed.
Pin.PULL_DOWN: Pull-down. Makes the value 0 when nothing is connected. Used when the button is connected to 3.3 V.
value: Reads the pin's value (no argument) or writes it (value(1) and so on). For an input, returns 0 or 1.
on: Sets the pin to 1 (3.3 V). An LED lights up.
off: Sets the pin to 0 (0 V). An LED goes off.
toggle: Swaps the pin between 0 and 1. Each call turns the LED on or off.
ADC: Turns an analog voltage into a number (A/D conversion). GP26–28 as in ADC(26), and the built-in temperature sensor with ADC(4).
read_u16: Reads the ADC value as an integer from 0 to 65535. 65535 corresponds to 3.3 V. voltage = value × 3.3 ÷ 65535.
I2C:
A class for using I2C (I-squared-C) communication. Talks to sensors over two wires.
The first 0 in I2C(0, sda=…, scl=…, freq=…) means use I2C number 0 of the Pico's two.
I2C.sda: The pin connected to the data line (SDA). For example sda=Pin(4) is GP4. Which pins can be used is fixed for I2C0 and I2C1.
I2C.scl: The pin connected to the clock (timing) line (SCL). For example scl=Pin(5) is GP5.
I2C.freq: The communication speed (Hz). 400000 is 400 kHz (fast mode). If reading fails, lowering it to 100000 can make it stable.
scan: Returns a list of the addresses of devices connected to I2C. If nothing appears, check the wiring.
readfrom_mem: readfrom_mem(address, register, number of bytes). Reads a value from a fixed place (register) in the sensor.
writeto_mem: writeto_mem(address, register, data). Writes a setting to a fixed place (register) in the sensor.
sleep: Waits for the given number of seconds. time.sleep(0.5) is 0.5 seconds.
sleep_ms: Waits for the given number of milliseconds. In MicroPython, time.sleep_ms(10) is 0.01 seconds; in C++ (Pico SDK), sleep_ms(500) waits 500 ms.
ticks_ms: The time since start-up (milliseconds). Calculate time differences with ticks_diff.
ticks_us: The time since start-up (microseconds). Measures more finely than ticks_ms.
ticks_diff: ticks_diff(newer time, older time) returns the difference between two times. It calculates correctly even when the value wraps around.
ticks_add: ticks_add(time, time to add) calculates a time a little after a given time. Used to run at fixed intervals.
collect: Cleans up memory that is no longer used (garbage collection). Call it when memory is short.
statvfs: Checks the size and free space of the storage (flash).
unpack: Turns bytes into numbers. In struct.unpack(">h", data), ">h" means "a big-endian signed 16-bit integer".
Serial: Opens a serial port from the PC (pyserial). serial.Serial(port, speed, timeout=…).
Serial.timeout:
The maximum number of seconds to wait when reading. With timeout=1, if no data comes within 1 second, it gives up and returns empty data.
If not given, it waits forever until data comes.
Serial.baudrate: The communication speed. The Pico's USB serial runs at the same speed whatever the value.
readline: Reads one line, up to a newline.
reset_input_buffer: Throws away received data that has not been read yet. Call it before starting to read, so you do not read old data.
decode.errors: What to do with bytes that cannot be turned into text. "ignore" skips them. "replace" turns them into ?. If not given, it raises an error.
reader: Reads a CSV file one line at a time, as a list of values.
print: Shows things on the screen (the output box).
print.sep: The text put between values. The default is one space. sep="," separates with commas.
print.end: The text added at the end. The default is a newline. end="" means no newline.
range: range(5) is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. range(1, 6) is 1 to 5. Sets how many times a for loop repeats.
len: Returns the length (number of items or characters).
append: Adds one item to the end of a list.
open: Opens a file. open(name, "w") is for writing, "a" for appending, and omitted for reading.
zip: Takes items from several lists at the same time, one at a time. Used like for a, b in zip(xs, ys):.
PWM:
A class for using PWM (pulse width modulation). Pass a pin, as in PWM(Pin(15)).
Turns on and off very fast to change an LED's brightness or a motor's speed.
freq: Frequency. How many times a second it repeats (Hz). For PWM, pwm.freq(1000) is 1000 times a second.
duty_u16: Sets PWM's "share of time on" from 0 to 65535. 0 is off, 32768 is half, 65535 is brightest.
deinit: Stops using it and returns the pin to how it was.
NeoPixel:
A class for using RGB LEDs (WS2812). The 1 in NeoPixel(Pin(23), 1) is the number of LEDs.
Set the color with np[0] = (red, green, blue) and light it with np.write().
flush: Writes data that has not been written yet to the file right away.
listdir: Returns a list of the file names in a folder. os.listdir() for the top folder.
stat: Returns information about a file. os.stat("log.csv")[6] is the file's size (bytes).
strftime: Turns a time into text. "log_%Y%m%d" gives something like log_20261105.
feature_importances_: In a decision tree, how much each feature contributed to the decisions. Features close to 0 can be removed.
$ sudo:
Origin: short for superuser do (run as the administrator).
Runs the following command with administrator rights. Needed to change system settings or install software.
It asks for your password the first time (nothing appears on screen as you type).
$ apt:
Origin: short for Advanced Package Tool.
The command that manages software on Ubuntu. It installs and removes software.
$ apt install:
Installs software from the internet.
Example: sudo apt install pipx installs pipx.
$ pipx:
Origin: pip with an x added. pip is the tool for installing Python software, and x is said to stand for execute.
A tool that installs commands written in Python so they do not mix with other things.
$ pipx install:
Installs a Python command.
Example: pipx install mpremote installs mpremote.
$ pipx ensurepath:
Origin: ensure (make sure) + path (the places commands are looked for).
Sets things up so commands installed with pipx can be typed from any folder. Open a new terminal for it to take effect.
$ python3-sklearn: The machine learning library scikit-learn. Used to train decision trees on the PC.
$ python3-serial: pyserial, a library for using serial ports from Python.
$ mpremote:
Origin: MicroPython + remote (operating from somewhere else).
MicroPython's official tool. Operates the Pico from the terminal.
Each command connects to the Pico automatically and disconnects when done. It cannot be used at the same time as Pico Studio.
$ mpremote version: Shows the version of mpremote itself. Used to check that it installed correctly.
$ mpremote connect:
Specifies the port to connect to.
Example: mpremote connect /dev/ttyACM1 ls lists the files on the Pico on that port.
$ mpremote connect list: Lists the serial ports connected to the PC.
$ mpremote exec:
Origin: exec is short for execute.
Runs the Python code in quotes (") on the Pico. Lets you try short code without making a file.
Similar to typing one line in Pico Studio's send box.
$ mpremote run:
Sends a file on the PC to the Pico and runs it. Corresponds to Pico Studio's "▶ 実行" (Run).
No file is left on the Pico.
$ mpremote soft-reset:
Origin: soft (without turning the power off) + reset.
Restarts MicroPython on the Pico. A running program stops.
Used instead of Pico Studio's "■ 停止" (Stop).
$ mpremote reset: Restarts the Pico. Corresponds to Pico Studio's "リセット" (Reset). If there is a main.py, it then runs automatically.
$ mpremote repl:
Origin: REPL is short for Read-Eval-Print Loop.
Opens a screen (the REPL) for talking to the Pico one line at a time. To finish, press Ctrl + ] or Ctrl + X.
$ mpremote df:
Origin: df is short for disk free.
Shows the size and free space of the Pico's storage, in bytes.
$ mpremote ls:
Origin: ls is short for list.
Lists the files on the Pico. Corresponds to Pico Studio's "ピコのファイル" (Files on the Pico).
$ mpremote cat:
Origin: cat is short for concatenate.
Shows the contents of a file on the Pico.
$ mpremote cp:
Origin: cp is short for copy.
Copies a file. The name with : in front is on the Pico.
PC → Pico is "save to Pico"; Pico → PC takes it out.
$ mpremote rm:
Origin: rm is short for remove.
Deletes a file on the Pico. It cannot be undone.
$ :: A leading : means "a file on the Pico". Without :, it is a file on the PC.
$ lsusb:
Origin: short for list USB.
Lists the USB devices connected to the PC.
$ lsusb -d:
Origin: -d is short for device.
Shows only devices from the given maker.
2e8a: is Raspberry Pi's vendor number.
$ 2e8a: Raspberry Pi's USB vendor number. The Pico can be identified by this number.
$ ls:
Origin: short for list.
Lists files and folders.
$ ls -l:
Origin: -l is short for long.
Lists in detail: permissions, owner, size and date.
$ lsblk:
Origin: short for list block devices. A block device reads and writes data in chunks, like a drive.
Lists the drives connected to the PC.
$ lsblk -o:
Origin: -o is short for output.
Specifies which columns to show.
$ NAME,LABEL: Shows two things: the drive's name and its label.
$ RP2: The text to look for. It is part of the drive name of a Pico in flashing mode (RPI-RP2).
$ dmesg:
Origin: said to be short for display message.
Shows the record of what happened inside the PC (the kernel log). It also shows USB plugging and unplugging.
$ dmesg -w:
Origin: -w is short for wait. The long form is --follow.
Keeps waiting for new records and shows them as they come. Stop with Ctrl + C.
$ grep:
Origin: short for global regular expression print.
Picks out only the lines that contain some text.
Example: | grep 2e8a keeps only the lines containing 2e8a.
$ |:
Origin: a pipe, like data flowing through a pipe.
Passes the result of the command on the left to the command on the right.
$ cp:
Origin: short for copy.
Copies a file. Write it as "cp source destination".
$ cd:
Origin: short for change directory.
Moves to another folder in the terminal.
$ cat:
Origin: short for concatenate (join together).
Shows the contents of a file.
$ rm:
Origin: short for remove.
Deletes a file. It does not go to the trash and cannot be undone.
$ python3:
Origin: version 3 of Python.
Runs a Python program on the PC.
$ udevadm:
Origin: short for udev admin. udev is short for userspace /dev, the system that manages devices.
The command that manages settings for USB devices and the like (udev rules).
$ udevadm control: Gives instructions to the running udev.
$ udevadm --reload-rules:
Origin: reload + rules, joined. Not an abbreviation.
Reloads the udev rules so new settings take effect.
$ ~/apps/pico-studio: The folder where Pico Studio is. ~ is your home folder.
$ ./start.sh: Runs start.sh in the current folder. Starts Pico Studio and opens the browser.
$ /dev/ttyACM0:
The Pico's serial port. Linux treats devices like files too.
A second one gets a higher number, such as ttyACM1.
$ /etc/udev/rules.d/: The folder for settings for USB devices (udev rules).
$ /etc/udev/rules.d/99-pico-studio.rules: An old settings file. Its number is too high for it to take effect, so delete it.
$ 70-pico-studio.rules: A settings file that lets the logged-in user use the Pico's port.
$ /run/media/$USER/RPI-RP2/: The drive of a Pico in flashing mode. $USER is replaced by your user name.
$ *.uf2: The MicroPython firmware file. * means "any characters", standing in for the version part.
$ hello.py: A file on the PC with the code you want to run. You choose the name.
$ log.csv: The name of the file made on the PC side.
$ pc_logger.py: A PC program that receives and saves the Pico's data (Chapter 15).
$ train.py: A PC program that trains the decision tree (Chapter 16).
import:
Loads a module (a bundle of features).
Example: import os makes os's features available.
os:
Origin: short for operating system.
A module that handles files and system information.
uname:
Origin: short for Unix name.
A function that returns system information. On the Pico, it shows the MicroPython version and the board name.
$ echo:
Origin: an echo.
Outputs the text you write as it is.
$ tee:
Origin: named after a T-shaped pipe junction (a tee).
Writes what it receives to a file while also showing it on screen.
Combined with sudo, it can create files in places only the administrator can write to.
$ rm -f:
Origin: -f is short for force.
Deletes without an error even if the file is missing, and without asking.
$ /etc/udev/rules.d/70-pico-studio.rules:
The settings file that decides permissions for the Pico's port.
The number 70 is the loading order; it only works if it comes before 73.
$ mkdir:
Origin: short for make directory.
Makes a folder.
$ mkdir -p:
Origin: -p is short for parents.
Also makes the folders along the way. No error if it already exists.
$ pwd:
Origin: short for print working directory.
Shows the folder you are in, in the terminal.
$ ~/apps/pico-code: An example folder for keeping code for the Pico. You may choose the name. ~ is your home folder.
$ ~/apps/pico-code/hello.py: The file of code to run, written with its full location.
$ ssh:
Origin: short for Secure Shell.
Logs in to a computer across the network. It cannot be used with the Pico.
$ scp:
Origin: short for secure copy.
Copies files to a computer across the network.
$ ssh -T:
Origin: -T means "do not use a terminal".
Does not log in; only checks that you can connect. ssh -T git@github.com tells you whether GitHub accepts your key.
$ ssh -vT:
Origin: -v is short for verbose.
Runs ssh -T while showing in detail what happens along the way. You can see which keys were tried and where you were refused.
$ ssh -A:
Origin: -A stands for agent forwarding.
Lets the machine you logged in to use the keys in your own PC's ssh-agent. The private key is not copied. Use it only on machines you manage yourself.
$ ssh git@github.com: GitHub's SSH entrance. The username is git for everyone; which account you are is decided by your key.
$ ssh git@github-collar: Connects using the nickname github-collar set in ~/.ssh/config (connects to github.com with the chosen key).
$ ssh-keygen:
Origin: short for key generator.
Makes an SSH key (a pair of a private key and a public key). It can also delete the stored key of a host you connected to (-R).
$ ssh-keygen -t:
Origin: -t is short for type.
Chooses the type of key. ed25519 is recommended today.
$ ssh-keygen ed25519: One type of key. Short, secure and recommended today. The files are id_ed25519 (private key) and id_ed25519.pub (public key).
$ ssh-keygen -C:
Origin: -C is short for comment.
A note attached to the key. Use a name that tells you which machine's key it is. It goes at the end of the public key.
$ ssh-keygen -f:
Origin: -f is short for file.
The name and location of the key file. Without it, the key is ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.
$ ssh-keygen -N:
Origin: -N stands for new passphrase.
Sets the passphrase. -N "" makes it empty (you are not asked).
$ ssh-keygen -R:
Origin: -R is short for remove.
Deletes the old record of that host's key from ~/.ssh/known_hosts. Use it when the other machine's OS has been reinstalled.
$ ssh-add: Adds a key to ssh-agent (the helper that remembers keys). Once added, you do not have to type the passphrase every time.
$ ssh-add -l:
Origin: -l is short for list.
Shows the list of keys ssh-agent remembers.
$ ssh-copy-id:
Origin: copy id means "copy my key (ID)".
Adds your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the other machine. From then on, you can ssh in without a password.
$ ~/.ssh: The folder for SSH keys and settings. It holds id_ed25519 (private key), id_ed25519.pub (public key), known_hosts (records of hosts you connected to), config (settings), authorized_keys (public keys allowed to log in) and so on.
$ ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub: The public key file. Register its one line of contents with GitHub. Fine to share.
$ ~/.ssh/config: The ssh settings file. For each host, you can write which key to use and a nickname.
$ ~/.ssh/collar_deploy: A key (private key) made with a name given by ssh-keygen -f. The one ending in .pub is the public key.
$ ~/.ssh/collar_deploy.pub: The public key of the key made with ssh-keygen -f. Register it under Deploy keys in the GitHub repository.
$ hostname: Shows this machine's name. Add .local after it, and machines on the same LAN can connect using that name.
$ hostname -I:
Origin: -I stands for IP address.
Shows this machine's IP address.
$ openssh-server: An ssh server. Once installed, other machines can log in to this machine with ssh.
$ exit: When you are logged in with ssh, logs out and returns to the original machine.
$ pi@raspberrypi.local:
The form "username@computer-name". Connects to raspberrypi.local as the user pi.
With scp, write the destination path after the : that follows.
$ pi@raspberrypi.local:/home/pi/: The destination computer and the folder on it.
$ nano: A text editor used inside the terminal. Ctrl + O saves, Ctrl + X quits.
$ systemctl:
Origin: short for system control.
The command that manages Linux services. The Pico does not have it.
$ systemctl enable: Sets a service to start automatically at boot.
$ systemctl --now: In addition to the setting, starts it running right now.
$ systemctl restart: Stops a service and starts it again.
$ journalctl:
Origin: short for journal control. A journal is a record.
Shows Linux logs.
$ journalctl -u:
Origin: -u is short for unit.
Shows only the logs of the given service.
$ logger: The name of the service used in this chapter's example.
$ logger.service: The name of the service's settings file in this chapter's example.
$ logger.py: The file of the program that records sensor data in this chapter's example.
$ main.py: main.py on the PC. Saved on the Pico under the same name, it runs automatically at power-on.
$ /etc/systemd/system/logger.service: The service's settings file. Put it in /etc/systemd/system/.
$ sh:
Origin: short for shell.
Runs a shell script.
$ deploy.sh:
Origin: deploy means to put in place.
A script that bundles the steps, used in this chapter's example.
$ mpremote mip:
Origin: said to be short for mip installs packages.
The system for installing MicroPython libraries onto the Pico.
$ mpremote mip install: Installs a library onto the Pico. Example: mpremote mip install library-name
$ pip:
Origin: said to be short for pip installs packages.
Installs Python libraries. It cannot be used on the Pico.
$ apt upgrade: Updates the installed software to newer versions.
writeto:
Sends data to an I2C device.
Example: i2c.writeto(0x44, bytes([0x24, 0x00])) sends 2 bytes to the device at address 0x44.
readfrom:
Reads data from an I2C device.
Example: i2c.readfrom(0x44, 6) reads 6 bytes from the device at address 0x44.
asyncio: A module that runs several tasks by taking turns. Within one program, it can make them look like they run at the same time.
asyncio.sleep: Waits for the given number of seconds. While waiting, other tasks can run. Use it with await.
asyncio.run: Starts running a task made with async.
create_task: Registers a task and starts running it in the background.
async: Put in front of def to make a task that can take turns (a coroutine).
await: Waits for a task to finish. While waiting, it gives other tasks their turn.
$ SUBSYSTEM==\"tty\", ATTRS{idVendor}==\:
The body of the udev rule.
Puts a mark called uaccess on serial ports (tty) with vendor number 2e8a, so the logged-in user can use them.
stdio_init_all:
Makes input and output such as printf usable (C++). Call it once at the start of main().
pico_enable_stdio_usb in CMakeLists.txt sends the output over USB.
printf:
Origin: short for print formatted.
Outputs text (C / C++). %d is an integer, %.2f a decimal with 2 places, %s a string, and \n a newline.
gpio_init: Prepares a pin for use as a GPIO (C++). Used together with gpio_set_dir.
gpio_set_dir: Decides whether a pin is an output (GPIO_OUT) or an input (GPIO_IN) (C++). Corresponds to MicroPython's Pin.OUT / Pin.IN.
GPIO_OUT: Output (C++). The program outputs 0 / 1. MicroPython's Pin.OUT.
GPIO_IN: Input (C++). Reads the pin's 0 / 1. MicroPython's Pin.IN.
gpio_put: Outputs 0 (false) or 1 (true) on an output pin (C++). Corresponds to MicroPython's pin.value(1).
gpio_get: Reads a pin's state (C++). true for 1, false for 0. MicroPython's pin.value().
gpio_pull_up: Turns on the pin's internal pull-up resistor (C++). It reads 1 when nothing is connected. MicroPython's Pin.PULL_UP.
gpio_set_function: Switches a pin's role (C++). GPIO_FUNC_I2C makes it an I2C pin, GPIO_FUNC_PWM a PWM pin.
GPIO_FUNC_I2C: The setting that makes a pin an I2C pin (C++). Corresponds to specifying the pins in MicroPython's I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), ...).
sleep_until: Waits until a set time (C++). Combined with a time made by delayed_by_ms, it lets you run at fixed intervals.
delayed_by_ms: Makes a time the given number of milliseconds after another time (C++). Corresponds to MicroPython's time.ticks_add.
get_absolute_time: Gets the current time (time since start-up) (C++). Returned as the type absolute_time_t.
absolute_time_diff_us: Returns the difference between two times in microseconds (C++). Written in the order absolute_time_diff_us(earlier, later). Corresponds to MicroPython's time.ticks_diff (with the arguments in the opposite order).
time_us_64: Returns the time since start-up in microseconds (C++). Corresponds to MicroPython's time.ticks_us. It does not wrap around, so you can subtract directly.
i2c_init: Prepares I2C (C++). i2c_init(i2c0, 400 * 1000) uses I2C0 at 400 kHz. Specify the pins separately with gpio_set_function.
i2c_write_blocking:
Sends data over I2C (C++). i2c_write_blocking(I2C, address, data, number of bytes, nostop).
If the last is true, the connection stays open so you can read next with i2c_read_blocking. Returns the number of bytes sent, or a negative number on failure.
i2c_read_blocking:
Reads data over I2C (C++). i2c_read_blocking(I2C, address, where to put it, number of bytes, nostop).
Returns the number of bytes read, or a negative number on failure.
i2c0: The first I2C unit (C++). GP4 (SDA) and GP5 (SCL) are used with i2c0. The 0 in MicroPython's I2C(0, ...).
adc_select_input: Chooses which ADC to read (C++). GP26 is 0, GP27 is 1, GP28 is 2, the built-in temperature sensor is 4.
adc_read: Reads the chosen ADC (C++). Returns a 12-bit value from 0 to 4095. MicroPython's read_u16() is 0–65535, so the range differs.
adc_set_temp_sensor_enabled: Enables the built-in temperature sensor (C++). Combine with adc_select_input(4).
multicore_launch_core1: Starts running a function on the second core (core 1) (C++). The function must never end. Needs pico_multicore in CMakeLists.txt.
stdio_usb_connected: true if the PC has opened the USB serial port (C++). Used to wait until the PC connects.
constexpr: Makes a constant whose value is decided at build time (C++). Used for pin numbers and the like, as in constexpr uint LED_PIN = 25;.
int16_t: A signed 16-bit integer (−32768 to 32767) (C / C++). Corresponds to "h" in struct.
uint8_t: An unsigned 8-bit integer (0 to 255). One byte (C / C++).
static_cast: Changes a type (C++). static_cast<int16_t>(x) treats x as an int16_t.
include:
Reads in another file (a header) (C / C++). Corresponds to MicroPython's import.
With "", it first looks in the same folder as the .cpp (for .h files you made and so on).
pragma: #pragma once is a marker that keeps the same header from being read twice (C / C++). Write it at the top of a header file.
#include <cstdio>: C++ standard library: text input and output. printf and so on.
#include <cstring>: C++ standard library: memory and string operations. memcpy, memset and so on.
#include <cmath>: C++ standard library: math functions. sqrtf, fabs and so on.
#include <cstdint>: C++ standard library: integer types with fixed sizes. uint8_t, uint32_t and so on.
#include <cstddef>: C++ standard library: basic types. size_t, offsetof and so on.
#include <cassert>: C++ standard library: assert. Stops if the condition is not true.
#include <algorithm>: C++ standard library: common algorithms. std::min, std::max, std::sort and so on.
#include <optional>: C++ standard library: std::optional. Expresses whether there is a value or not.
#include <pico/stdlib.h>: Pico SDK basics. gpio_put, sleep_ms, stdio_init_all and so on.
#include <hardware/adc.h>: Pico SDK ADC (analog input). adc_init, adc_read and so on.
#include <hardware/pwm.h>: Pico SDK PWM. pwm_set_wrap, pwm_set_gpio_level and so on.
#include <hardware/i2c.h>: Pico SDK I2C. i2c_init, i2c_read_blocking and so on.
#include <hardware/pio.h>: Pico SDK PIO (freely programmable input/output circuits). Used inside ws2812.h.
#include <hardware/clocks.h>: Pico SDK clocks (CPU speed). clock_get_hz, set_sys_clock_khz and so on.
#include <hardware/flash.h>: Pico SDK functions for writing to flash. flash_range_erase, flash_range_program and so on.
#include <hardware/sync.h>: Pico SDK functions for stopping interrupts. save_and_disable_interrupts and so on.
#include <hardware/watchdog.h>: Pico SDK watchdog. watchdog_enable, watchdog_update and so on.
#include <pico/sync.h>: Pico SDK locks that protect data between cores. critical_section, mutex and so on.
#include <pico/multicore.h>: Pico SDK functions for using the second core. multicore_launch_core1 and so on.
#include <pico/cyw43_arch.h>: Pico SDK support for the Pico W's wireless chip. cyw43_arch_init, cyw43_arch_gpio_put and so on.
#include <pico/binary_info.h>: Pico SDK system for putting a name and version into a program. bi_decl and so on.
#include <pico/unique_id.h>: Pico SDK functions for reading each Pico's unique number. pico_get_unique_board_id_string and so on.
#include <mpu6050.h>: A class that comes with Pico Studio for reading the MPU6050 (accelerometer and gyro) (Chapter 11).
#include <ws2812.h>: A class that comes with Pico Studio for lighting an RGB LED (Chapter 8).
#include <filter.h>: An example of a header you make yourself. The moving-average class MovingAverage (Chapter 13).
#include <sht31.h>: An example of a header you make yourself. The declaration of the SHT31 class (Chapter 13).
#include <model.h>: A header you make yourself. The classification function predict made by train.py (Chapter 16).
#include <features.h>: A header you make yourself. The function features that calculates features (Chapter 19).
pico_sdk_init: Prepares the Pico SDK (CMakeLists.txt). Write it after project() and before add_executable().
target_link_libraries: Specifies the libraries a program uses (CMakeLists.txt). pico_stdlib is the basics, hardware_i2c is I2C, hardware_adc is the ADC.
pico_enable_stdio_usb: Whether to send printf output to USB serial (CMakeLists.txt). 1 sends it. Without it, /dev/ttyACM0 does not appear.
pico_add_extra_outputs: Also makes the .uf2 file for flashing and so on (CMakeLists.txt).
$ cmake:
Reads CMakeLists.txt and creates the build steps (a Makefile).
cmake .. means "use the CMakeLists.txt in the folder one level up".
$ cmake -DPICO_BOARD=pico2: Builds with the board type set to Pico 2. The Pico W is pico_w and the Pico 2 W is pico2_w.
$ make: Builds using the steps cmake created. make blink builds only blink.
$ make -j4:
Origin: -j is short for jobs.
Runs 4 jobs at the same time to make the build faster.
$ git: Software that records changes to source code. It keeps track of when and what changed, lets you go back to an earlier state, and lets you put code on GitHub.
$ git clone: Downloads a whole repository (a complete set of source code) from the internet.
$ git clone --branch: Specifies the version (branch or tag) to download.
$ git submodule: Works with other repositories used inside a repository (submodules).
$ git submodule update: Downloads the submodules. With --init, it also does the preparation needed the first time.
$ git init:
Origin: init is short for initialize.
Makes the current folder managed by git. A hidden folder called .git is created inside. Only once per project, at the start.
$ git add: Picks the changes to go into the next commit.
. means "the current folder".
Puts every change in the current folder into the next commit (except what is listed in .gitignore).
$ git commit:
Origin: commit means to fix something in place, to put it on record.
Saves the changes picked with git add as one record (a commit). You can go back to this state later.
$ git commit -m:
Origin: -m is short for message.
Write the commit description inside quotes ("). Example: git commit -m "Add I2C reading"
$ git push: Sends (uploads) your local commits to GitHub.
$ git push --tags: Also sends the markers made with git tag to GitHub. git push alone does not send them.
$ git pull: Brings new commits on GitHub into your local repository. Used to get changes made on another PC.
$ git diff:
Origin: diff is short for difference.
Shows uncommitted changes line by line. - is a removed line, + is an added line.
$ git restore: Returns a file to its last committed state. Uncommitted changes are lost and cannot be recovered.
$ git tag:
Origin: a tag is a label, like one tied to luggage.
Puts a named marker such as v1.0.0 on the current commit. Lets you find and take out a version you shipped later.
$ git --init: Also does the preparation needed the first time. git submodule update --init prepares and downloads the submodules in one go.
$ git --version: Shows git's version. If it shows one, git is installed.
$ git config:
Origin: config is short for configuration.
Makes or shows git settings.
$ git config --global: Makes the setting apply to all repositories of this user on this PC. It is written to ~/.gitconfig. Without it, the setting applies only to the current repository.
$ git --list: Shows a list of the settings.
$ git user.name: The name recorded in commits.
$ git user.email: The email address recorded in commits. Once on GitHub, anyone who looks at the commits can see it. If you do not want to show it, use the noreply address shown under GitHub's Settings → Emails.
$ git init.defaultBranch: The name of the first branch of repositories made with git init. Make it main, the same as GitHub.
$ git pull.rebase:
Origin: rebase means "to change the base".
How git pull combines things when both sides changed. false means merge (adds one record that combines them).
$ git pull.rebase false: When both sides changed, git pull combines them with a merge. It is easy to see what happened, so start with this.
$ git core.editor: The editor that opens when you write a commit description and so on. With nano, Ctrl + O → Enter saves, and Ctrl + X closes.
$ git status: Shows the list of changed files, staged files and new files, and whether you are ahead of GitHub. When in doubt, start with this.
$ git diff --staged: Shows the changes put on the stage with git add (what goes into the next commit).
$ git log:
Origin: a log is a record or diary.
Shows the commit history, newest first. Quit with q.
$ git log --oneline: Shows each commit on one line, with just its number (first 7 characters) and description.
$ git log -p:
Origin: -p is short for patch (the difference made by a change).
Also shows what each commit changed. Add a file name to see only that file.
$ git show: With a commit number, shows that commit's description and what it changed.
$ git remote: Works with remotes (repositories somewhere else, such as GitHub).
$ git remote -v:
Origin: -v is short for verbose.
Shows the names and URLs of the registered remotes.
$ git remote add: Registers a remote with a name. git remote add origin URL registers the URL under the name origin.
$ git remote set-url: Changes the URL of a registered remote. For example, when switching from HTTPS to SSH.
$ git origin: The name of a remote. By convention, the GitHub repository is called origin. When you clone, it gets this name automatically.
$ git main: The name of the main branch. New repositories made on GitHub use main.
$ git master: The name of the main branch used in older repositories. Today, main is normal.
$ git push -u:
Origin: -u is short for upstream (where the branch connects to).
Makes git remember where this branch connects. After that, git push and git pull alone are enough. Add it only the first time.
$ git --delete: git push origin --delete name deletes a branch on GitHub.
$ git switch: Switches branches. The files in the working folder change to that branch's state.
$ git switch -c:
Origin: -c is short for create.
Makes a new branch and moves to it.
$ git switch --detach: Leaves the branch and moves to the state of a commit number or tag. Use it just for looking; to go back, git switch main.
$ git branch: Shows the list of branches. The one with * is the branch you are on.
$ git branch -d:
Origin: -d is short for delete.
Deletes a branch. Branches that have not been merged are not deleted (so you do not lose important changes).
$ git branch -D: Forcibly deletes even branches that have not been merged. Commits that existed only on that branch can no longer be seen.
$ git branch -m:
Origin: -m is short for move (here, rename).
Renames a branch. git branch -m master main renames master to main.
$ git merge: Brings the changes of the named branch into the branch you are on.
$ git merge --abort: Stops a merge that has conflicts and returns to the state before it.
$ git restore --staged: Takes something off the stage. The changes to the file stay as they are.
$ git restore --source: Takes out a file as it was in the given commit and replaces the current file with it.
$ git commit --amend: Remakes the last commit (fix its description or add something you forgot). Do not use it after pushing.
$ git --no-edit: Keeps the commit description as it is.
$ git revert: Makes a new commit that cancels the changes of the given commit. The history is not erased, so you can use it even after pushing.
$ git stash: Sets aside uncommitted changes for a while and returns to the state of the last commit.
$ git stash pop: Brings the changes set aside with git stash back into the working folder.
$ git rm:
Origin: rm is short for remove.
Deletes a file and puts that deletion into the next commit.
$ git rm --cached: Removes the file only from git's record. The file on your PC is not deleted. Use it for files you recorded before writing them in .gitignore.
$ git rm -r:
Origin: -r is short for recursive.
Applies to everything inside the folder.
$ git --cached: Removes the file only from git's record. The file on your PC is not deleted.
$ git clone --bare: Copies it as a repository with only the record and no working folder. Used as storage that other machines push to (the same form as the ones inside GitHub).
$ git --allow-unrelated-histories: Allows combining two repositories that started separately. Used when connecting to a repository made on GitHub with a README.
$ git -m:
Origin: -m is short for message.
Write the commit description inside quotes (").
$ git reset: Returns commits or the stage to an earlier state. Depending on how it is used, records can be erased, so until you understand it, use git restore or git revert.
$ git reset --hard: Forcibly returns both the working folder and the stage to the given commit's state. Uncommitted changes are lost and cannot be recovered. Do not use it.
$ git push --force: Overwrites GitHub's record with your local record. Commits that existed only on GitHub are lost. Do not use it.
$ git try-sleep: An example branch name (a branch for trying sleep mode). You can freely name branches with letters, digits and -.
$ &&:
If the previous command succeeded, runs the next one.
git add . && git commit -m "…" is the same as typing the two in order.
$ gh:
Origin: short for GitHub.
GitHub CLI. The official command for working with GitHub from the terminal. The first time, log in with gh auth login.
$ gh repo:
Origin: repo is short for repository.
Works with GitHub repositories.
$ gh repo create: Makes a new repository on GitHub.
$ gh --private: Makes a repository that only you (and people you invite) can see. To let anyone see it, use --public.
Makes the repository from the current folder (.).
$ gh --push: After making the repository, sends the current folder's commits to GitHub.
$ gh auth:
Origin: auth is short for authentication.
Handles gh's login to GitHub.
$ gh auth login: Logs in to GitHub. You choose SSH or HTTPS for git operations, and with SSH it can even register your public key.
$ gh auth status: Shows the account you are logged in with and the method used for git operations (ssh or https).
$ gh config:
Origin: config is short for configuration.
Makes gh settings.
$ gh config set: Changes a setting. Written as gh config set name value.
$ gh git_protocol: Whether repositories made or cloned with gh use ssh or https URLs.
$ gh git_protocol ssh: Uses SSH URLs (git@github.com:…). For when your SSH key is registered with GitHub.
$ gh repo view: Shows the repository's description and README.
$ gh repo clone: Clones a GitHub repository. For your own repository, the name alone is enough, without the username.
$ collar: The project name used in this chapter's example (a program for a cow collar). Replace it with your own project's name.
$ code:
The command that starts VS Code from the terminal.
code collar opens the collar folder in VS Code. code . opens the current folder.
$ .gitignore: A file listing the files git should not record. One per line: folders like build/, or patterns like *.csv. Everything after # is a note.
Opens the current folder in VS Code.
$ code --install-extension: Installs a VS Code extension by its name (ID).
$ ms-vscode.vscode-serial-monitor: The name (ID) of Microsoft's "Serial Monitor" extension. Shows the Pico's printf output inside VS Code.
$ ms-vscode.cpptools-extension-pack: The name (ID) of Microsoft's "C/C++ Extension Pack". Installs C/C++ completion and error display, CMake Tools and more together.
$ usernamehw.errorlens: The name (ID) of the "Error Lens" extension. Shows errors and warnings as text to the right of the line.
$ mhutchie.git-graph: The name (ID) of the "Git Graph" extension. Shows the commit history as a branching diagram.
$ mechatroner.rainbow-csv: The name (ID) of the "Rainbow CSV" extension. Colors CSV files by column.
$ github.vscode-github-actions: The name (ID) of the "GitHub Actions" extension. Shows the results of automatic builds on GitHub in VS Code.
$ ms-ceintl.vscode-language-pack-ja: The name (ID) of Microsoft's "Japanese Language Pack". Puts VS Code's menus in Japanese.
$ export: Sets an environment variable. export PICO_SDK_PATH=... tells the build where the SDK is.
$ source: Loads settings written in a file into the current terminal. source ~/.bashrc makes settings you just added usable right away.
$ picotool: A tool for operating the Pico over USB. It can flash .uf2 files and show information about the Pico. Built together with the Pico SDK.
$ picotool load: Flashes a program to the Pico. -x runs it after flashing, -f switches to flashing mode automatically if it is not already.
$ python3 -m: Runs a Python module as a command. python3 -m serial.tools.miniterm runs pyserial's serial monitor.
$ serial.tools.miniterm: A serial monitor included in pyserial. Shows the Pico's printf output and sends text. Stop with Ctrl + ].
$ flash.sh: A script that does everything from building to flashing.
$ blink.uf2: The file made by building blink.cpp, for flashing to the Pico.
gpio_pull_down: Turns on the pin's internal pull-down resistor (C++). It reads 0 when nothing is connected. MicroPython's Pin.PULL_DOWN.
gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback:
Enables a pin's interrupt and sets the function to call (C++).
gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(pin, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true, &function) calls the function the moment it changes from 1 to 0 (Chapter 14).
GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL: When the pin changes from 1 to 0 (C++). When a pull-up button is pressed.
GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_RISE: When the pin changes from 0 to 1 (C++). When a pull-up button is released.
add_repeating_timer_ms:
Makes a timer that calls a function at fixed intervals (C++).
add_repeating_timer_ms(-10, function, nullptr, &timer) is every 10 ms. A minus sign means the interval is counted "from the previous start" (Chapter 14).
make_timeout_time_ms: Makes a time the given number of milliseconds from now (C++).
to_ms_since_boot: Turns a time (absolute_time_t) into a number of milliseconds since start-up (C++). Corresponds to MicroPython's time.ticks_ms(). Wraps around after about 49 days.
getchar_timeout_us: Receives one character from USB (C++). If none arrives within the given microseconds, returns PICO_ERROR_TIMEOUT.
adc_gpio_init: Switches a pin to analog input (C++). Only GP26–29 can be used.
pwm_gpio_to_slice_num: Returns the number of the PWM circuit (slice) a pin uses (C++). Two pins share one slice.
pwm_set_wrap: Sets the largest number counted in one PWM period (C++). It counts from 0 to this number and goes back to 0.
pwm_set_clkdiv: Sets how fast PWM counts (C++). It counts at the CPU clock divided by this number.
pwm_set_gpio_level: Sets PWM's share of time on (C++). 0 is off; the same number as wrap is brightest.
GPIO_FUNC_PWM: The setting that makes a pin a PWM pin (C++).
flash_range_erase: Erases flash (C++). Place and size are multiples of 4096. Erased bytes become 0xFF. Stop interrupts while doing it (Chapters 15 and 17).
flash_range_program: Writes to flash (C++). The size is a multiple of 256. You can only write to places that have been erased.
save_and_disable_interrupts: Stops interrupts and returns the previous state (C++). Restore it with restore_interrupts. Stop them only for a short time.
watchdog_enable: Starts the watchdog (C++). With watchdog_enable(2000, true), it restarts if watchdog_update() is not called within 2 seconds (Chapter 17).
watchdog_update: Signals "I'm alive" to the watchdog (C++). Call it at intervals shorter than the set time.
watchdog_caused_reboot: true if the previous restart was caused by the watchdog (C++).
set_sys_clock_khz: Changes the CPU clock (speed) (C++). set_sys_clock_khz(48000, true) gives 48 MHz. Slower uses less power (Chapter 17).
clock_get_hz: Returns a clock's speed (Hz) (C++). clock_get_hz(clk_sys) is the CPU speed.
multicore_fifo_push_blocking: Sends a 32-bit number to the other core (C++). If full, waits until there is room (Chapter 14).
multicore_fifo_pop_blocking: Receives a number that arrived from the other core (C++). Waits until one arrives.
critical_section_enter_blocking: Takes a lock (C++). Keeps other cores and interrupts from touching the same data. Release it with critical_section_exit.
critical_section_exit: Releases a lock taken with critical_section_enter_blocking (C++).
cyw43_arch_init: Prepares the Pico W's wireless chip (C++). The Pico W's LED can be used after this too.
cyw43_arch_gpio_put: Outputs to a pin connected to the Pico W's wireless chip (such as the LED) (C++). cyw43_arch_gpio_put(CYW43_WL_GPIO_LED_PIN, true) turns the LED on.
pico_get_unique_board_id_string: Returns each Pico's unique number (unique ID) as a string (C++) (Chapter 19).
bi_decl: Puts information (name, version and so on) into the program (C++). It can be read with picotool info (Chapter 19).
volatile: A marker meaning "this variable may change at any time" (C / C++). Put it on variables changed in interrupts. Without it, old values may keep being seen.
struct: Makes a type that bundles several values together (C / C++). Written like struct Record { uint32_t ms; float ax; };.
enum: Makes a list of named values (C / C++). Written like enum class Mode { Idle, Run };, it is used as Mode::Idle.
uint: An unsigned integer (0 to about 4.3 billion) (C++). Used for pin numbers and the like in the Pico SDK.
uint16_t: An unsigned 16-bit integer (0 to 65535) (C / C++). ADC values and the like.
uint32_t: An unsigned 32-bit integer (0 to about 4.3 billion) (C / C++). Times (milliseconds) and the like.
uint64_t: An unsigned 64-bit integer (C / C++). Microseconds from time_us_64() and the like.
sqrtf: Square root (for float) (C / C++). sqrt is for double and slow on the Pico.
memcpy: Copies the contents of memory as they are (C / C++). memcpy(destination, source, number of bytes).
assert: If the condition is not true, stops there and shows the line number (C / C++). Used in tests (Chapter 19).
$ arm-none-eabi-size: Shows the size of a Pico program. text is flash use, and data + bss is RAM use (Chapter 13).
$ g++: The C++ compiler for the PC. Makes programs that run on the PC, not the Pico (the tests in Chapter 19).
$ openocd: Software that connects the Pico and the debugger (gdb) through a Debug Probe (Chapter 19).
$ gdb-multiarch: Software that stops a program partway so you can investigate while looking at variables (a debugger). It works for ARM programs too (Chapter 19).
$ picotool info: Shows information about the program on the Pico (name, version, build date and time). -a shows everything.
$ picotool reboot: Restarts the Pico. With -u it restarts into flashing mode (BOOTSEL); -f forces it even while a program is running.
$ make -C:
Origin: -C is short for change directory.
Builds in the given folder. make -C build builds in the build folder.
$ cmake -S:
Origin: -S is short for source.
Specifies the folder that has CMakeLists.txt.
$ cmake -B:
Origin: -B is short for build.
Specifies the folder to put the build output in.
$ mpremote bootloader: Puts a Pico running MicroPython into flashing mode (BOOTSEL).
#include <iostream>: C++ input and output such as cout and cin
#include <vector>: std::vector, an array whose length can change
#include <thread>: Threads, and waiting such as sleep_for
#include <chrono>: Lengths of time (milliseconds and so on)
int: The integer type (usually 32 bits, about ±2.1 billion)
unsigned: Makes an integer with no minus values (unsigned)
char: The type for one character (1 byte)
double: The decimal type (double precision, about 15 digits)
float: The decimal type (single precision, about 7 digits). On microcontrollers it is often faster than double
bool: The type for true or false
void: "Nothing". Used for functions with no return value
auto: Lets the compiler decide the type from the right-hand side
static: Inside a function, "a variable that does not disappear between calls"; inside a class, "only one, not one per object"
inline: A hint that the function's body may be expanded where it is called. Used when writing functions in a header
explicit: Stops a constructor from doing type conversions on its own
sizeof: The size of a type or variable (in bytes)
using: Lets you leave out a namespace name (using namespace std;), or gives a type another name
std: The namespace of the C++ standard library (used like std::cout)
main: The function where the program starts
return: Returns the function's answer and ends the function
if: Runs only when the condition is true
else: Runs when the condition is not true
for: Repeats a set number of times. for (initialization; condition; update)
while: Repeats while the condition is true
do: do { } while (condition); a loop that always runs at least once
break: Leaves a loop or a switch
continue: Skips the rest of the loop and goes to the next round
switch: Branches by value. Combined with case
case: One value's case inside a switch (case value:)
default: In a switch, when no case matches
class: A class (a blueprint bundling data and functions)
public: Can be used from outside the class
private: Can only be used from inside the class
this: In a member function, a pointer to "this object itself"
template: Makes a function or class whose type is decided later (a template)
typename: Declares the name of a template's type (template <typename T>)
new: Makes an object on the heap and returns a pointer (delete it when done)
nullptr: A pointer that points to nothing
reinterpret_cast: Reads the contents of memory as a different type (a dangerous conversion; used when touching hardware)
try: Wraps code where an exception may occur
vector: An array whose length can change (std::vector<int> and so on)
map: Key–value pairs (std::map). Kept in key order
strcmp: Compares C strings (0 if they are the same)
memset: Fills memory with a given value
fabs: The absolute value of a decimal
optional: A type expressing whether there is a value or not (std::optional)
size_t: An unsigned integer type for sizes and counts
sleep_for: Waits for a set length of time
from: Loads only part of a module. from datetime import date
as: Gives another name to something imported, or something opened with with
def: Makes a function. After def name(arguments):, write the body indented
in: In for, "one at a time from..."; in a condition, "whether it is in..."
or: True when at least one is true
is: Whether two things are the same object. Used to check for None, as in x is None
pass: Does nothing (put where the grammar needs something)
match: Branches by the shape of a value (from Python 3.10). Combined with case
except: What to do when an error occurs inside try. You can specify the kind, as in except ValueError:
with: Opens a file or the like and closes it automatically when done
input: Reads one line from the keyboard (returned as a string)
list: Makes a list (an ordered, changeable container)
set: Makes a set (a container with no duplicates)
str: A string. str(3) turns a number into a string
type: Checks the type of a value
pop: Takes an item out of a list and removes it (the last one if no position is given)
remove: Finds that value in a list and removes it
values: The list of a dictionary's values
get: Gets a value from a dictionary. If the key is missing, returns None (or the second argument)
strip: Removes spaces and newlines at both ends
join: Joins the strings in a list with text in between. ", ".join(names)
format: Puts values into a string (f"..." f-strings do the same)
pi: π, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter
json: A module for reading and writing JSON files
load: Reads a JSON file into dictionaries and lists
csv: A module for reading and writing CSV (comma-separated) files
writer: Makes a tool for writing CSV
ZeroDivisionError: The error when you divide by 0
KeyboardInterrupt: The exception raised when you stop with Ctrl + C
TypeError: The error when types do not match (adding a string and a number and so on)
pip: The tool for installing Python libraries
$ apt update: Refreshes the list of software (which versions are available). Do it before apt install
Loads a settings file into the current terminal (the same as source)
$ python3 -c: Runs the following string as Python code
$ journalctl -f: Keeps showing new log lines as they come
$ git --branch: Chooses the branch (or tag) to fetch
$ g++ -Wall: Shows all warnings about common mistakes
$ g++ -o: Sets the name of the executable to make
random: A module that makes random numbers. Used like random.randint(1, 6).
randint: randint(a, b) returns a random whole number from a to b, inclusive. randint(1, 6) is like rolling a die.
cyw43_arch_enable_sta_mode: Puts the Pico W's wireless into the mode that joins a Wi-Fi router (station) (C++).
cyw43_arch_wifi_connect_timeout_ms: Connects to Wi-Fi (C++). cyw43_arch_wifi_connect_timeout_ms(name, password, security type, ms to wait). Returns 0 when connected.
CYW43_AUTH_WPA2_AES_PSK: The Wi-Fi security type. This is the one for ordinary home or barn routers (WPA2 password).
cyw43_wifi_link_status: Returns the state of the Wi-Fi link (C++). CYW43_LINK_JOIN means connected.
cyw43_arch_lwip_begin: Call lwIP (network) functions between this and cyw43_arch_lwip_end (C++). With Background lwIP, it stops them clashing with the work done in the background.
cyw43_arch_lwip_end: Ends the section started with cyw43_arch_lwip_begin (C++).
ipaddr_aton: Turns a text IP address such as "192.168.1.10" into lwIP's ip_addr_t (C++).
ip_addr_t: The lwIP type that holds an IP address (C++).
udp_new: Makes the holder (udp_pcb) used to send with UDP (C++, lwIP).
udp_pcb: The lwIP type for a UDP holder. Made with udp_new.
udp_sendto: Sends data with UDP (C++, lwIP). udp_sendto(holder, data, destination IP, port).
pbuf_alloc: Gets a buffer (pbuf) to hold data for lwIP to send (C++). Give it back with pbuf_free when done.
pbuf_free: Gives back a buffer got with pbuf_alloc (C++).
vsnprintf: Writes values received as a va_list into a char array using a format (C / C++). Used to make your own function written like printf.
snprintf: Writes to a char array instead of the screen, the same way as printf (C / C++). snprintf(array, size, format, …). Never writes past the size.
sscanf: Reads values out of text (C / C++). sscanf(line, "aim %d %d", &a, &b) returns how many it read (2 here).
va_list: Points to arguments of unknown number received with "…" (C / C++). Start with va_start and finish with va_end.
PICO_ERROR_TIMEOUT: A marker meaning nothing arrived in the time allowed (C++). Returned by getchar_timeout_us and others.
clk_sys: The clock the CPU uses (C++). clock_get_hz(clk_sys) tells you its speed.
acos: Gives the angle (in radians) from a cosine (C / C++). Multiply by 57.3 to get degrees.
fmin: Returns the smaller of two values (C / C++).
absolute_time_t: The Pico SDK type for a point in time (C++). Returned by get_absolute_time and delayed_by_ms.
#include <cstdarg>: For arguments of unknown number (va_list, va_start, va_end).
socket: Makes an endpoint for talking over the network (Python's socket). socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) is UDP over IPv4.
SOCK_DGRAM: Means send with UDP (socket). TCP is SOCK_STREAM.
bind: Starts receiving on a chosen port (socket). ("", 5005) receives on port 5005 for any IP address.
recvfrom: Waits until one piece of UDP data arrives (socket). Returns (data, sender).
sendto: Sends data with UDP (socket). sendto(bytes, (IP, port)).
ThreadingHTTPServer: A small web server built into Python. It handles page requests that arrive at the same time separately.
BaseHTTPRequestHandler: The base class for handling requests to the web server. Write do_GET and it is called when someone opens a page.
do_GET: The function called when a browser opens a page (BaseHTTPRequestHandler).
send_response: Sends the response code (BaseHTTPRequestHandler). 200 means OK.
end_headers: Sends the end of the headers (BaseHTTPRequestHandler). Write the body after this.
wfile: Where to write the body sent back to the browser (BaseHTTPRequestHandler). self.wfile.write(bytes).
log_message: The function that logs each request (BaseHTTPRequestHandler). Make it pass to log nothing.
serve_forever: Runs the web server until it is stopped.
Thread: Runs a function in a separate flow (thread) (threading). With daemon=True it ends when the main program ends.
escape: Turns <, > and & into forms that show as plain text in HTML (html.escape).
Path: Represents the location of a file or folder (pathlib). Join with /, as in Path.home() / "barn-data".
mkdir: Makes a folder (pathlib). With exist_ok=True it is not an error if it already exists.
choice: Picks one item from a list at random (random.choice).
startswith: Checks whether text starts with some text (Python).
encode: Turns text into bytes (Python). Used before sending or writing.
datetime: The date and time module (Python). datetime.datetime.now() gives the current time.
#include <PicoCamera.h>: The PicoCamera camera library (Appendix I). git clone it into the project and add add_subdirectory(PicoCamera) and pico_camera to CMakeLists.txt.
add_subdirectory: Also reads the CMakeLists.txt in another folder and builds the library in it (CMakeLists.txt).
pico_camera: The name of the PicoCamera library (add it to target_link_libraries in CMakeLists.txt).
camera_config_t: A type holding the camera settings (PicoCamera). Fill in the GP numbers, picture format, size and so on, and pass it to pico_camera_init().
pin_sccb_sda: The GP the camera's SIOD is connected to. Like I2C SDA, an even GP.
pin_sccb_scl: The GP the camera's SIOC is connected to. Like I2C SCL, an odd GP.
pin_vsync: The GP the camera's VSYNC (picture starts) is connected to.
pin_href: The GP the camera's HREF (line starts) is connected to.
pin_pclk: The GP the camera's PCLK (next byte) is connected to.
pin_xclk: The GP that sends the clock to the camera. Made with the Pico's PWM.
pin_d0: The GP the camera's D0 is connected to. D0–D7 must be eight in a row (pin_d1 is pin_d0 + 1 …).
pin_reset: The GP the camera's RESET is connected to. -1 means the Pico does not drive it.
pin_pwdn: The GP the camera's PWDN (power-off) is connected to. -1 means the Pico does not drive it.
xclk_freq_hz: Speed of the clock sent to the camera (Hz). 10000000 is 10 MHz.
sccb_i2c_port: Which I2C (0 or 1) is used for the camera settings. 0 for GP12 and GP13.
pixel_format: The picture format. PIXFORMAT_JPEG gives a JPEG.
PIXFORMAT_JPEG: Receive pictures as JPEG. The OV2640 can make JPEGs inside the camera (the OV7670 cannot).
frame_size: The picture size. FRAMESIZE_QVGA is 320×240, FRAMESIZE_VGA is 640×480.
jpeg_quality: JPEG quality (0–63). Smaller is sharper and gives more data.
fb_count: How many places (frame buffers) to hold pictures. 1 on the Pico, which has little memory.
pico_camera_init: Finds the camera, sets it up and reserves memory for a picture (PicoCamera). Returns PICO_CAMERA_OK if it works.
pico_camera_err_t: PicoCamera's result type. PICO_CAMERA_OK means success; anything else is an error number.
pico_camera_err_str: Turns an error number into a description (PicoCamera). Print it to see the cause.
pico_camera_sensor_info_get: Returns information (such as the name) about the camera found (PicoCamera). ->name gives a name like OV2640.
pico_camera_fb_get: Takes one picture and returns where it is (camera_fb_t) (PicoCamera). nullptr if it fails.
camera_fb_t: A picture taken (PicoCamera). buf is the data, len the number of bytes, width and height the size.
pico_camera_fb_return: Gives back the place used by a picture (PicoCamera). If you don't, the next picture cannot be taken.
pico_camera_sensor_get: Returns the tool (sensor_t) for changing camera settings (PicoCamera).
sensor_t: A type grouping the functions that change camera settings (PicoCamera). Used like s->set_vflip(s, 1).
set_vflip: Flips the picture upside down (1 to flip, 0 for normal). set_hmirror flips left to right.
stdio_put_string: Sends text or data of a given length over USB (C++). With false at the end it does not turn \n into \r\n, so it can send data such as pictures.
stdio_flush: Sends any data still waiting, straight away (C++).
cv2: The Python module for OpenCV (a library for pictures and video). Install it with sudo apt install python3-opencv.
imdecode: Turns data such as a JPEG back into an image (a table of colours, one per dot) (OpenCV). None if it cannot be read.
imshow: Shows an image in a window (OpenCV). The first argument is the window name.
waitKey: Redraws the window and waits the given milliseconds for a key (OpenCV). Returns the number of the key pressed.
frombuffer: Turns bytes into a numpy array. With np.uint8 it is a row of numbers from 0 to 255.
ord: Returns the number of a character (Python). ord("s") is 115. Used to compare with the result of waitKey.
$ git clone --depth: Downloads only the latest version (--depth 1). Faster when you don't need the history.
